newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - Firms find new ways to tap teen market.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Firms find new ways to tap teen market.

text.p: Frustrated by traditional marketing efforts to reach today's teenagers, a handful of companies are taking to the streets, using grassroots tactics in an effort to gain influence and create excitement about their products.

Although record companies have used street marketing for years as a means of promoting new artists, the marketing teams behind some major companies ranging from soft drinks to watches have begun adopting the approach.

"Marketers are just waking up to it," said Janine Misdom, partner at Sputnik, a New York trend-tracking and market research firm specialising in urban youth. "You're seeing bigger and bigger brands learning how to do it."

Athletic shoe makers are at the forefront of this trend. To promote the release this week of its Dennis Rodman All Star 91 basketball shoe, the athletic footwear maker Converse Inc has hired a team of 10 urban youths to "seed" the market. For $350 a week, the youths -- hand-picked for their influence in the neighbourhoods and their knowledge of both fashion and basketball -- distribute stickers and display advance versions of the new Rodman shoe.
"They're all very clued into the fashion and basketball enthusiast market in the market where they're from," said Jim Solomon, Converse's senior vice president of global marketing.

Solomon said his company also has a team seeding the shoes with high school and college basketball teams, which are less driven by fashion than on-court performance. "We believe in the grassroots," said Solomon.
Converse will back the All Star 91, named after Rodman's uniform number, with a major TV, radio and outdoor advertising campaign featuring the infamous Chicago Bulls rebounder.
OTHER SUCCESFUL CAMPAIGNS
Converse's seeding teams follow in the successful footsteps of rivals Reebok and L.A. Gear, both of which have used the practice to target their brands to young consumers.

L.A. Gear Inc, based in Santa Monica, California, has hired Asylm Marketing, a Los Angeles company specialising in promoting recording artists, to apply its street savvy to promoting two new shoe brands: Mongo, aimed at hip 16-to-28-year-olds, and Digit 3, a shoe for skateboarding and other action board sports.
The company tapped its network of 150 strategically selected youths in 90 cities to promote the products, with the next wave of the launch beginning July 1.

"I'm a firm believer that perception is reality. We really work on creating perception, which sometimes is more important than creating reality," said Scott Leonard, a partner at Asylm, which helped promote a number of record artists including Bush, Bjork, Live and Smashing Pumpkins.

Leonard said more mainstream companies are coming to him with help in reaching teens. In addition to the L.A. Gear launch, Asylm is working on the introduction of Spoon, a new watch brand from Seiko Corp aimed at the board sports community.

In another grassroots effort, PepsiCo Inc's Mountain Dew this summer has teamed with hip-hop music bible The Source magazine, sponsoring a 13-city van tour. Six specially equipped, $150,000 vans will go to neighbourhood haunts, spreading the word on the latest in urban fashion and distributing the newest music, T-shirts and, of course, Mountain Dew.

Black Entertainment Television and 10 record companies also have signed up for the tour, which will appear in parks, church picnics, parades and school playgrounds. "It's not only reaching them where they live, but where they hang out," said Jon Harris, a spokesman for Pepsi's Mountain Dew.

"We know that our consumers see through commercialisation and over-commercialisation," said Harris. "Teaming up with The Source provides a great vehicle to connect with consumers in a meaningful way."

Although Pepsi could have sponsored a sampling tour of its own, teaming with The Source allows the marketer to align itself with the magazine's hip-hop image in a more authentic way. And authenticity in reaching teens is essential, said Jeff Jones, The Source's associate publisher. "It's gotta ring true. Otherwise, you're worse off than you were before. You're better off going with your regular advertising than saying, 'We're hip. We're cool. We've got big baggy shorts,'" Jones said.

Asylm's Leonard added: "Teens are very suspect of corporate America. It's really important they are spoken to in a way that does not insult them. Too often, marketers don't understand their target. They're close, but off just a little."
TEEN PREFERENCES COULD LAST WITH AGE

For marketers such as Converse, Seiko and Pepsi, teens represent a particularly attractive target, controlling $103 billion in spending last year, said Peter Zollo, president of Teenage Research Unlimited in Northbrook, Illinois. "Unlike Generation X, who are paying off college debt, generation Y -- these teens -- don't have any payments to hold them down so they can blow their money on whatever they want," Zollo said.

Consumers also tend to shape brand preferences during their teen years, Zollo said, a trend underscored by Mountain Dew's own consumer profile. Although the soft drink is aimed at teens and young adults, 30-to-39-year-olds represent a third of total brand volume. "While we say teens and young adults are the target, many people continue to take their Dew drink habits with them when they age," Harris said.
And because teens say their No. 1 source for trend information is not media, but other teens, grassroots marketing efforts are particularly effective, Zollo said.
"The trick is, you need those trend-setters," Jones said. "It's the city mice that make it happen."
